title: Parent material

definition.text: The underlying geological material, generally bedrock or a superficial (drift) deposit, in which soil horizons form.

facts.text: Soils inherit much of their structure and minerals from it, so they are often classified by whether it is consolidated and how it was last transported.
It may be igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic bedrock or unconsolidated glacial, river or volcanic deposits; for metamorphic rock the original rock is the protolith.
Rock is the source of all soil minerals and of every plant nutrient except nitrogen, hydrogen and carbon.
Typical parent minerals include quartz, calcite, feldspar and mica (biotite).
Its nature strongly shapes the soil: mudstone or shale give clay-rich soils, while sandstone weathers into sandy soils.
Parent materials are classed by how they were deposited: residual (weathered in place), transported (by water, wind, ice or gravity) or cumulose (organic matter accumulated in place).
Weatherable minerals in the parent rock favour mull humus, while a shortage of them is associated with moder.
Parent material strongly influences how many basic ions a soil contains.

notes: Merges Parent material, Parent rock (assigned to How soils form) and Soil formation#Parent material, which describe the same concept.

title: Residuum

definition.text: Weathered rock that stays in place rather than being moved by erosion, and in time helps form soil.

facts.text: It is purely mineral, unlike organic parent materials, and is not moved by wind, water or gravity.
Soils formed from it, residual soils, are expected to resemble their underlying bedrock in mineralogy and general chemistry.
Regolith covers all unconsolidated material above bedrock, transported sediments included, whereas residuum is strictly untransported.
Saprolite keeps the structural features of its bedrock; residuum has lost them, having been transformed further and shrunk in volume.
It forms mainly by chemical weathering in every climate: a thin blanket over bedrock in temperate regions, much thicker in the tropics.
Residual soils imply landscape stability; in the United States as little as three percent of soils are residual.
In limestone terrain the bedrock–residuum boundary is sharp but irregular, with pinnacles of fresh rock in reddish residual silts and clays; resistant chert or sandstone remains as float.

notes: Also covers Parent material#Consolidated (residual parent material). S:01b4f719704f (volume decrease) is tagged citation needed.

title: Transported parent material

definition.text: Loose, uncemented parent material moved by water, wind, ice or gravity, and classified by its last means of transport.

facts.text: Most soils form in transported material moved many miles by wind, water, ice and gravity.
Material carried by a glacier and then redeposited by streams is named for its last agent, as stream-transported or glacial fluvial parent material.
Recognized modes are wind (aeolian), water, gravity (colluvial), ice (glacial till), lakes (lacustrine) and oceans (marine).
Wind moves silt and fine sand hundreds of miles to form loess, but seldom moves clay, which forms stable aggregates.
Wind also carries sand-sized particles, typically as dunes, and volcanic ash that settles at various distances from a volcano.
Water-transported materials are classed as alluvial, lacustrine or marine.
A decrease in rock fragments with depth, especially over saprolite, suggests the soil material has moved downslope.

notes: S:d14297ce9799 (volcanic tephra) is tagged citation needed.

title: Glacial till

definition.text: Unsorted sediment eroded and carried by a glacier and deposited directly from the ice.

facts.text: Not carried by liquid water, it is unsorted and unstratified: mostly clay, silt and sand with scattered pebbles, cobbles and boulders, often in a bimodal size distribution.
Basal till, laid beneath the glacier, is typically very compact and slow to take in water; ablation till, dropped as the ice melts, is less compacted.
It is deposited in terminal, lateral, medial and ground moraines, and in drumlins and flutes.
Its clasts often come from outcrops hundreds of kilometres away and are faceted, striated or polished by glacial abrasion.
Archibald Geikie first applied the term to primary glacial deposits in 1863; the older name boulder clay has fallen out of favour.
Melting glaciers rework till into glaciofluvial outwash and glaciolacustrine or glaciomarine deposits such as varves.
Till follows its source rock: sandstone gives loose sandy till, granite and gneiss stony gravelly till, and limestone, clay or shale the clayey till typical of boulder clay.
Boulder clay is tough, compact and overconsolidated, from its fine rock flour and the weight of overlying ice.

notes: Till is crawled but outside the scope set; Parent material#Glacial till (Morainal) covers the same material. S:3ffa18762df9 (ablation till less compacted) is tagged citation needed.

definition.text: Boulders, gravel, sand, silt and clay from ice sheets or glaciers that meltwater streams have transported, sorted and deposited.

facts.text: They are laid down beside, below or downstream from the ice.
Retreating glaciers leave outwash plains as alluvial deposits are carried downstream from the ice.
Much of North America and Europe is underlain by Pleistocene sand and loess derived from glacial outwash.

definition.text: Parent material formed from glacier-derived sediment carried into lakes, typically lakes at the ice margin.

facts.text: Inflowing rivers drop their larger rocks and stones near the lake edge, while suspended sediment settles across the whole lake bed.
Annual deposition can leave clear layers called varves.

definition.text: Sediment that settled in lakes, forming a well-sorted, fine-textured parent material rich in silt and clay.

facts.text: Its high clay content gives the soils formed in it low permeability.
Beach ridges may mark where ancient lakes once washed up sand.
Lake Bonneville and many soils around the Great Lakes are examples.

definition.text: Material carried by rivers to the sea that sank to the ocean floor and later became a parent material.

facts.text: Soils along the US Gulf Coast and in California's Imperial Valley formed on ancient sea beds exposed as the land was uplifted.
Glaciomarine sediments, delivered to the ocean by glaciers or icebergs, may hold large ice-dropped boulders amid fine-grained sediment.

definition.text: Organic parent material built up in place from plant residues, such as sphagnum moss, preserved by a high water table or other conditions that slow decay.

facts.text: It includes peat and muck soils, preserved by the low oxygen content of a high water table.
Peat may form sterile soils, while muck soils may be very fertile.
Unlike other parent materials it is not moved but originates from deposited organic material.

title: Volcanic tephra parent material

definition.text: Volcanic ash carried by the wind and settled at various distances from a volcano, the most common volcanic parent material.

facts.text: Volcanic ash and lava flows interbedded with unconsolidated material are part of Earth's regolith.
Soils of siliceous ash consist of glass bubbles and shards with high internal surface area, and weather rapidly to imogolite and smectite.
These andisols are highly fertile, rich in organic matter and of particularly low bulk density.
Volcanic ash is also a source of non-glacial loess, as in Ecuador and Argentina.

notes: S:d14297ce9799 (the definition line) is tagged citation needed.

definition.text: A blanket of loose, unconsolidated and varied surface deposits covering solid rock.

facts.text: It includes dust, broken rock and related materials and occurs on Earth, the Moon, Mars, some asteroids and other terrestrial planets and moons.
George P. Merrill defined it in 1897, from Greek rhegos, blanket, and lithos, rock, for the whole mantle of unconsolidated material whatever its origin.
On Earth it originates from weathering and biological processes and ranges from absent to hundreds of metres thick.
Its age ranges from instantaneous, for fresh ash or alluvium, to hundreds of millions of years, as with Precambrian regolith in parts of Australia.
Its uppermost part, which typically holds significant organic matter, is what is conventionally called soil.
It comprises transported cover, saprolith, interbedded volcanic deposits, duricrust, groundwater salts and biota.
Few plants grow in solid rock and animals need loose material to burrow, so regolith underpins most life.
It matters to engineers, hosts mineral deposits, supplies sand, gravel, lime and gypsum, and is the zone through which aquifers recharge and discharge.

title: Asteroid regolith

definition.text: The loose surface layer of asteroids, produced by impacts and other surface-altering processes.

facts.text: Spacecraft show it ranges from fine-grained deposits to coarse, boulder-rich debris.
Hayabusa's samples from Itokawa were the first asteroid regolith grains studied in the laboratory, showing space weathering and solar-wind implantation.
Hayabusa2 returned samples from Ryugu in 2020 and OSIRIS-REx from Bennu in 2023; both show organic- or carbon-rich material and water.

notes: A section of the Regolith seed; Soils beyond Earth may prefer to own it.

title: Icy regolith on Titan

definition.text: Loose icy material on Saturn's moon Titan, called regolith because it behaves mechanically like regolith on other bodies.

facts.text: The term traditionally covered only loose mineral grains or rock fragments; ice grains were left out because, as snow on Earth, they melt and fuse easily.
Titan is so cold that ice behaves like rock, giving an ice regolith with erosion and aeolian or sedimentary processes.
Huygens' penetrometer data suggest a surface better described as a sand of ice grains, on a plain covered in somewhat rounded pebbles.

notes: A section of the Regolith seed; Soils beyond Earth may prefer to own it.

definition.text: Chemically weathered rock, literally 'rotten rock', formed in the lower zones of soil profiles by deep weathering of the bedrock surface.

facts.text: It commonly keeps the structural details of its bedrock and inherits the texture, pH and minerals of its parent material.
Hydrolysis, chelation, hydration and freeze–thaw turn granite and other rocks into it; quartz's resistance can leave sandy soils, a process called arenization.
In the regolith, upper saprolite is fully oxidised bedrock, lower saprolite is reduced, partly weathered rock, and saprock is fractured bedrock weathered only along fractures.
Its colour comes mainly from iron compounds: fine goethite is yellow and coarse goethite brown; fine hematite is red and coarse hematite grey to black.
More intense weathering grades continuously from saprolite into laterite, whose first weathering products are kaolinized saprolites.
Being younger than its parent rock and older than any thick cover such as lava, it can sometimes be dated relatively.
Burrowing plants and animals bring saprolite up from depth to the surface.
Poorly weathered saprolite grit forms aquifers in Western Australia that can yield groundwater fit for livestock.

definition.text: Long-continued chemical weathering that builds thick, deeply weathered regolith over bedrock, the product of a region's long weathering history.

facts.text: It needs relief gentle enough to prevent erosion and allow leaching, long tectonic stability, and a humid tropical to temperate climate where warmth speeds reactions.
At weathering rates of 20 m per million years, deep regoliths take several million years to form; cooler climates need longer.
Deeply weathered profiles are widespread between latitudes 35°N and 35°S, and in parts of Africa, India, South America, Australia and southeast Asia regolith has formed for over 100 million years.
Regoliths range from a few metres to over 150 m thick, depending on surface age, tectonics, climate history and bedrock.
Sulfides and carbonates leach readily, while nickel, cobalt, copper and zinc in ferromagnesian minerals stay higher and reprecipitate with iron–manganese oxides in mid to lower saprolite.
It produces secondary and supergene ores: bauxite, iron ores, saprolitic gold, supergene copper, uranium and residual heavy minerals.
Weathering formed thin kaolinitic saprolites 1,000 to 500 million years ago, thick ones 200 to 66 million years ago, and medium-thick immature ones 5 million years ago in Sweden.

definition.text: The solid rock beneath the weathered rock and loose surface deposits, together called regolith, in the near-surface crust of Earth or another terrestrial planet.

facts.text: An exposed patch of bedrock is an outcrop; the top of the bedrock, where it meets the overlying material, is the rockhead.
Locating rockhead by digging, drilling or geophysics is important in most civil engineering projects; it can lie hundreds of metres down.
Exposed bedrock weathers physically or chemically, becoming susceptible to erosion; at its buried upper boundary, subsurface weathering forms saprolite.
Fragments detached from the bedrock and found within a weathering or soil profile are called floaters.
Geological maps show bedrock types as if all soil and superficial deposits were removed, unless the deposits are too thick to map through.
In the mapping of superficial deposits, all pre-Quaternary deposits count as bedrock.

title: Superficial deposits

definition.text: Geologically recent, mostly unconsolidated deposits, typically of Quaternary age (less than 2.6 million years old).

facts.text: They include stream channel and floodplain deposits, beach sands, talus gravels, glacial drift and moraine, raised beaches and brickearth.
Mostly gravel, sand, silt and clay, onshore they form relatively thin, often discontinuous patches.
Geological surveys keep databases of their properties, used in farming and forestry to judge erosion, growing conditions and the risk of nutrient leaching.

notes: Crawled but outside the scope set; passes the 2+ pages test (Parent material, Bedrock, Superficial deposits).

definition.text: In geology, deposits and soils derived from weathering in place, or from weathering plus gravitational movement or accumulation.

facts.text: In geology the removed material is irrelevant; the eluvial deposit is what remains.
Eluvial ore deposits such as tungsten and gold placers are enriched by winnowing away lighter material; diamonds in weathered kimberlite can count as eluvial too.
Brazil's Pitinga tin deposit, an eluvial deposit, is one of the largest tin mines in the world.
Supergene weathering of an apatite-rich carbonatite in Ontario produced a significant eluvial phosphate ore.

definition.text: A clastic, predominantly silt-sized sediment formed by the accumulation of wind-blown dust.

facts.text: Loess or similar deposits cover ten percent of Earth's land area.
It holds 20% or less clay with roughly equal parts sand and silt, typically 20 to 50 micrometres in grain size, and is often loosely cemented by calcium carbonate.
It is homogeneous, porous, friable, pale yellow or buff and usually unstratified; its angular grains of quartz, feldspar and mica let it stand in vertical banks.
Deposits exceed a hundred metres in north-western China, reaching 350 m on the Loess Plateau, and tens of metres in the US Midwest.
Pye (1995) gave four requirements: a dust source, enough wind to carry it, a place to accumulate, and time.
Von Leonhard described Löss along the Rhine in 1823–1824 and Lyell popularized the term in 1834; its wind-blown origin was recognized later, notably by von Richthofen in China (1878).
Its vertical cleavage lets it be dug into cave dwellings in parts of China.

image.caption: Wilson44691, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

definition.text: Loess blown from the floodplains of glacial braided rivers that carried meltwater and sediment from melting ice sheets and ice caps.

facts.text: As meltwater dwindled each autumn and winter, the bare floodplains dried and wind winnowed their glacially ground silt and clay, depositing it downwind.
The loess along both sides of the Mississippi River alluvial valley is a classic example.
The northern European loess belt, from southern England to southern Ukraine, shows strong periglacial influence; in England periglacial loess is called brickearth.
Loess ridges aligned with last-glacial winds are called paha ridges in America and greda ridges in Europe.

definition.text: Loess that originates from deserts, dune fields, playa lakes or volcanic ash rather than from glacial outwash.

facts.text: Varieties include desert loess from aeolian abrasion of quartz grains, volcanic loess in Ecuador and Argentina, tropical loess and trade-wind loess.
China's thick loess deposits were blown in from deserts in the north of the country.
Loess on the Great Plains of Nebraska, Kansas and Colorado is considered non-glacial desert loess, as is loess in Australia and Africa.

title: Loess soils and fertility

definition.text: Soils developed on loess, which tend to be very rich and, under suitable climates, among the most agriculturally productive in the world.

facts.text: The fine grains weather quickly because of their large surface area; fertility comes mainly from high cation exchange capacity and porosity rather than organic matter.
Soils underlain by loess tend to be excessively drained.
Even well-managed loess farmland can erode at well over 2.5 kg/m2 per year; Iowa's Loess Hills at times lost over 10 kg/m2 per year under autumn mouldboard ploughing.
Iowa's Loess Hills owe their fertility to 10,000 years of prairie humus; once that topsoil erodes, the loess beneath is infertile without fertilizer.

notes: S:a0ca8bcc488c (fertility not from organic matter) is tagged clarification needed, and S:d4c70f02f8b9 (underlying loess infertile) sits awkwardly beside the 'very rich soils' claim; worth a look in verification.

definition.text: A plateau of some 640,000 km2 around the upper and middle reaches of China's Yellow River, covered by loess.

facts.text: Its soil has been called the most highly erodible soil on Earth.
Loess in its banks gave the Yellow River its name and colour; farmed for over a thousand years, it has produced phenomenal yields.
It holds the thickest known loess deposit, up to 350 m.
Wind-borne loess particles contribute to the Asian Dust pollution problem.

title: Loess–paleosol sequences

definition.text: Stacked loess layers separated by buried soils, studied as archives of past climate and environmental change.

facts.text: In China the loess layers were laid down by a strong north-west winter monsoon, while the paleosols between them record a moist south-east monsoon.
Without robust numerical dating, even the position of the last interglacial soil in Austrian and Hungarian loess stratigraphies was long a matter of debate.
Since the 1980s luminescence methods have dated when grains were last exposed to daylight; SAR protocols give last-glacial ages with an accuracy of up to 5 and 10%.
Radiocarbon dating gives reliable loess ages for the last 40–45 ka when suitable in situ organic material such as charcoal or snail shells is found.

notes: Not marked contested: S:a05aa0b9b973 (flagged CONTESTED) reports a past dating dispute that luminescence dating has since eased, not a live debate.

title: Alluvium

definition.text: Loose clay, silt, sand or gravel deposited by running water in stream beds, on floodplains, in alluvial fans or similar settings.

facts.text: It is usually geologically young and unconsolidated; sediments laid down in seas, estuaries, lakes or ponds are not called alluvium.
Floodplain alluvium can be highly fertile and supported some of the earliest human civilizations.
Alluvial parent materials form on floodplains stratified by seasonal floods, in alluvial fans that coarsen toward the uplands, and in fine-grained deltas at river mouths.
Most alluvium is Quaternary and is often called 'cover' because it hides the bedrock beneath.
Antoine Furetière's dictionary, published in 1690, defined alluvion as new land formed by sediment along rivers and seas.
In the 19th century it meant river sediment above older 'diluvium', ascribed to Noah's flood; once that idea was rejected, diluvium became 'older alluvium'.
Because running water deposits it, alluvium is generally fine-grained and well sorted, unlike colluvium.

contested_note: Geologists still disagree over which sediment deposits, beyond those laid down by rivers, the term alluvium should include.

title: Colluvium

definition.text: Loose, unconsolidated sediment deposited at the base of hillslopes by rainwash, sheetwash, slow downslope creep or a combination of these.

facts.text: It is a heterogeneous mix of rock types and sizes, from silt to rock fragments, typically angular and loosely consolidated.
It accumulates as gently sloping aprons or fans at the foot of slopes or in gullies and hollows, sometimes several metres thick.
Gravity-moved parent material is obvious at the base of steep slopes as talus cones.
Thick colluvium often holds buried soils, plant and animal remains and archaeological deposits, recording long-term climatic change.
It differs from alluvium in not involving running water, and is poorly sorted where alluvium is well sorted.
Where the source material is fine and uniform, it can be hard to tell which process laid down a deposit.
Calcisols, cambisols and durisols develop mostly in alluvial and colluvial deposits, with aeolian deposits for the first two.

notes: S:ed2eea4aa28f (thickness, buried soils) is tagged citation needed.

definition.text: An elongated, unvegetated band of mostly talus-like basalt rock along a hillside or at the base of a cliff; also called a lava stringer.

facts.text: They occur mainly in north central Oregon at 900 to 1,100 m, a few metres to over 150 m long, 0.3 to 3 m wide and 20 to 65 cm deep.
They are thought to have formed under Quaternary periglacial conditions, through frost action, surface erosion, eluviation and mass wasting.
Intense freeze–thaw cycles probably sorted the rock debris, and frost penetrating no deeper than about 1 m explains their shallowness.
On level ground the same processes form stone rings around soil mounds, which grade into stripes as slope increases.

title: River channel migration

definition.text: The lateral shift of an alluvial river channel across its floodplain over time.

facts.text: It is driven mainly by bank erosion combined with point bar deposition on the opposite side of the channel.
Corkscrew-like helicoidal flow around bends undercuts banks into cut banks and moves sediment across the channel.
Cut-bank erosion usually equals point-bar deposition, and point bars push flow into the opposite bank, so meanders become better defined over time.
Its typical features are point bars, cut banks, meanders, floodplains and oxbow lakes.

notes: Assigned by the concept graph through Alluvium; fluvial geomorphology rather than soil science.

definition.text: Any naturally occurring solid mass or aggregate of minerals or mineraloid matter.

facts.text: Rocks are categorized by the minerals they contain, their chemical composition and how they formed.
They make up the Earth's crust and most of its interior, apart from the liquid outer core and pockets of magma.
The three main groups are igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks.
Sedimentary rocks form from sediments made by the weathering, transport and deposition of existing rocks.
Sediments, from smallest to largest, are clay, silt, sand and gravel.

definition.text: One of the three main rock types, formed by the cooling and solidification of magma or lava.

facts.text: It solidifies either below the surface as intrusive rock or at the surface as extrusive rock.
Intrusive igneous rocks have visible mineral grains, while extrusive ones are glassy or very fine-grained.
It is classified chiefly by particle size, which depends largely on cooling history, and by mineral composition.
Near the surface, acidic soil water and groundwater readily dissolve and break down igneous rocks, which are unstable there.

definition.text: Rock formed by the cementation of mineral or organic particles deposited at the Earth's surface.

facts.text: Its mineral detritus comes from the weathering and erosion of existing rocks, carried by water, wind, ice or mass movement.
It covers 73% of the Earth's land surface but makes up only about 8% of the crust's volume.
Clastic sedimentary rocks are cemented rock fragments, commonly grains of quartz, feldspar, clay minerals or mica, subdivided by dominant particle size.
Mudrocks contain at least 50% silt- and clay-sized particles.

definition.text: Rock transformed from an existing rock into a new type by heat and pressure, a process called metamorphism.

facts.text: The protolith is heated above 150 to 200 °C, often under 100 megapascals or more, and recrystallizes while staying mostly solid.
The protolith may be igneous, sedimentary or older metamorphic rock.
Metamorphic rocks form 12% of the Earth's land surface; examples are gneiss, slate, marble, schist and quartzite.

definition.text: The geological concept describing the transitions, through geologic time, among sedimentary, metamorphic and igneous rock.

facts.text: Each rock type changes when forced out of its equilibrium conditions; basalt, for example, breaks down and dissolves at the atmosphere.
Plate tectonics and the water cycle drive it.
Weathering and erosion break exposed rock into fragments and carry away dissolved material on the way to sedimentary rock.
On planets with life it is a biogeochemical cycle as well as a geologic one.

definition.text: The description of a rock unit's physical characteristics visible at outcrop, in hand or core samples, or under low magnification.

facts.text: The characteristics include colour, texture, grain size and composition.
Lithology can also mean a summary rock name such as sandstone, slate, basalt or limestone.
It is the basis for dividing rock sequences into lithostratigraphic units for mapping and correlation.
Site investigations describe it in standard terms, as in the European geotechnical standard Eurocode 7.

definition.text: A mineral that formed during the original crystallization of its host igneous rock and has not been chemically altered since.

facts.text: Soil minerals are of two types: primary minerals are found in soil but not formed there, while secondary minerals form as primary minerals weather.
Primary mineral particles are mostly larger than 2 μm, so they make up the silt, sand and gravel fractions.
Igneous rocks contain primary minerals such as quartz, feldspar, plagioclase, muscovite, biotite, amphibole, pyroxene and olivine.
Silicates dominate the primary minerals in soil; quartz and cristobalite are common soil tectosilicates.
Primary rocks are the source of primary minerals, which are in turn the components of parent rocks.

title: Feldspar

definition.text: A group of rock-forming aluminium tectosilicate minerals that also contain cations such as sodium, calcium, potassium or barium.

facts.text: Feldspars make up about 60% of the Earth's crust and 41% of the continental crust by weight.
The commonest are the sodium–calcium plagioclase feldspars and the potassium–sodium alkali feldspars.
Chemical weathering by hydrolysis turns feldspars into clay minerals including illite, smectite and kaolinite.
Hydrolysis starts with feldspar dissolving, which goes best in acidic or basic solutions, and the dissolution rate sets the weathering rate.
Because feldspars are so abundant, clays are very abundant weathering products and an important component of soils.
Formed at high temperature, feldspars, especially plagioclase, are unstable at the surface, so they weather easily to clays.
Clay-replaced feldspar looks chalky beside glassy unweathered grains; feldspar-rich sediment points to little chemical weathering before burial.
Orthoclase and microcline are potassium feldspars (KAlSi3O8) with the same composition but different crystal forms, monoclinic and triclinic; K-Na feldspars grade to albite as the alkali feldspars.

notes: Extends existing Feldspar entry; new facts only.

sources.title: 3.1: Soil Mineralogy - Geosciences LibreTexts (Digging into Canadian Soils)

definition.text: A continuous solid-solution series of framework silicate minerals within the feldspar group.

facts.text: The series runs from albite, NaAlSi3O8, to anorthite, CaAl2Si2O8, with sodium and calcium substituting for each other.
It is abundant in igneous and metamorphic rock and common as a detrital mineral in sedimentary rock.
Plagioclase weathers relatively rapidly to clay minerals such as smectite, so sandstones usually hold more of the more resistant alkali feldspar.
In hand samples it is often recognized by polysynthetic twinning, a set of fine parallel striations.

definition.text: A potassium feldspar, KAlSi3O8, an important tectosilicate mineral of igneous rock.

facts.text: It is a type of alkali feldspar, also called potassium feldspar or K-spar.
It is a common constituent of most granites and other felsic igneous rocks.
It commonly alters to sericite or clay.

definition.text: A common group of dark phyllosilicate minerals in the mica group, approximately K(Mg,Fe)3AlSi3O10(OH,F)2.

facts.text: Its sheets of iron, magnesium, aluminium, silicon, oxygen and hydrogen are weakly bound together by potassium ions.
It occurs in a wide variety of igneous and metamorphic rocks and makes up as much as 7% of the exposed continental crust.
It is greenish to brown or black, turning even yellow when weathered.

definition.text: A magnesium iron silicate mineral, (Mg,Fe)2SiO4, of the nesosilicate type.

facts.text: The main component of the upper mantle, it is common underground but weathers quickly at the surface.
It is among the least stable common surface minerals in the Goldich dissolution series, so it is rarely found in sedimentary rock.
With water it readily alters to iddingsite, a mix of clay minerals, iron oxides and ferrihydrite.
Speeding its weathering, for example by spreading fine olivine on beaches, has been proposed as a cheap way to sequester CO2.

definition.text: Describing silicate minerals, magmas and igneous rocks rich in magnesium and iron and relatively low in silica.

facts.text: Common mafic minerals are olivine, pyroxene, amphibole and biotite; common mafic rocks are basalt, diabase and gabbro.
Mafic and felsic materials are opposite ends of a compositional spectrum; mafic rocks are dark and dense, felsic ones light and less dense.
Chemically, mafic rocks have 45 to 55 wt% silica and are enriched in iron, magnesium and calcium; felsic rocks are enriched in aluminium, silicon, potassium and sodium.
The term, from magnesium and ferric, was coined in 1912.

definition.text: A carbonate sedimentary rock made mostly of calcite and aragonite, and the main source of lime.

facts.text: About 20% to 25% of sedimentary rock is carbonate rock, most of it limestone; much of the rest is dolomite.
Partly soluble, especially in acid, it erodes into karst landscapes of pavements, caves and gorges.
Water and organic acid from the soil slowly widen its joints over thousands or millions of years, dissolving the calcium carbonate.
Pulverized limestone is used as agricultural lime to neutralize acidic soils.

definition.text: An accumulation of angular, coarse sand and gravel produced by the granular disintegration of crystalline rocks, especially granitoids, through weathering.

facts.text: It forms by chemical and mechanical weathering, generally in arid or semiarid regions.
Cemented grus sand forms the sandstone arkose.
Most Late Cenozoic saprolite mantles in Europe are grus, unlike older Mesozoic and Early Cenozoic saprolites of kaolinitic and ferrallitic material.

definition.text: All sediment, from clay to boulders, carried by a glacier and deposited by or from the ice or by its meltwater.

facts.text: It is split into unstratified drift, or till, which forms moraines, and stratified drift laid down by meltwater as outwash plains, eskers, kames and varves.
In the United Kingdom drift is used more widely for all Quaternary surficial deposits mapped apart from bedrock, including loess, river deposits and colluvium.
Murchison introduced the term in 1839, after Lyell's idea that the sediments were dropped by drifting sea ice; the name outlived the hypothesis.

definition.text: Any accumulation of unconsolidated glacial debris, often till, in currently or formerly glaciated regions.

facts.text: It ranges from boulders down to gravel and sand in a groundmass of fine clayey glacial flour.
Lateral moraines form at the side of the ice, terminal moraines at its foot, marking the glacier's furthest advance.
Ground moraines are till-covered sheets of gently rolling relief under 10 meters, laid at the ice base as lodgment till.
Recessional moraines are small ridges left where a retreating glacier paused.

definition.text: A plain of glaciofluvial deposits built by meltwater outwash at the end of a glacier; also called a sandur.

facts.text: Meltwater sorts the sediment: boulders settle near the terminal moraine and the finest silt travels furthest.
Braided streams rework its surface, and kettle lakes form where buried ice blocks melted.
Fossil sandar, no longer active, lie in formerly glaciated areas.

title: Volcanic ash

definition.text: Fragments of rock, mineral crystals and volcanic glass under 2 mm across, produced by volcanic eruptions.

facts.text: Coarser explosive products are included in tephra, the fragmental material of an eruption whatever its composition or size.
Wind can carry ash thousands of kilometres.
Washed into the soil, ash minerals form a nutrient-rich andisol layer that is very good for farming.
Heavy ashfalls can bury pasture and sterilize the soil by oxygen deprivation; rehabilitation includes mixing ash with the buried soil.

notes: Covers the Tephra page too (S:dc01a3233ee2); tephra layers also date paleoenvironmental records (S:83a58dc9fcf3).

definition.text: The part lichens, symbiotic colonies of algae or cyanobacteria and fungi, play in breaking down rock and building and stabilizing soil.

facts.text: Lichens degrade minerals chemically and disrupt them physically, slowly turning rock into soil.
Metal-binding exudates and new minerals, especially metal oxalates, make them important agents of chemical weathering that create fertile soil from stone.
They are often the first settlers where there is no soil, at high elevations and latitudes.
In deserts, lichen crusts stabilize sand and hold water, and some plant seeds establish only there.

definition.text: Chemical weathering of jointed bedrock that produces concentric shells of highly decayed rock within saprolite; also called onion-skin weathering.

facts.text: Water enters along joints, so blocks weather inward fastest at corners, then edges, then faces, leaving a rounded core.
The cores, called corestones or woolsacks, are left as freestanding boulders or tors once erosion strips the saprolite.
Alteration forms secondary minerals such as kaolinite and montmorillonite and increases the rock's volume.
It has often been wrongly attributed to physical weathering alone; much of it happened in past humid, even tropical, climates.

title: Desert varnish

definition.text: An orange-yellow to black coating, about one micrometre thick, on exposed rock surfaces in arid environments.

facts.text: It forms only on stable rock surfaces no longer exposed to frequent rain, fracturing or wind abrasion, and is made mainly of clay with iron and manganese oxides.
The clay can only arrive by wind; it traps other substances that react together when the rock heats in the sun, with wetting by dew also important.
Black varnish holds manganese 50 to 60 times more abundantly than the crust's 0.12%; one proposed cause is manganese-oxidizing microbes.
Where the micro-environment pH exceeds 7.5, orange varnishes poor in manganese but rich in iron develop instead.

notes: A 2008 study (S:0b1b0dfad357) holds that the main component is silica rather than clay; the contrast with the clay view is noted but not treated as a formal debate.

definition.text: Hydrolysis is any chemical reaction in which a water molecule breaks one or more chemical bonds.

facts.text: In hydrolysis one fragment of the split molecule gains a hydrogen ion and the other gains a hydroxide.
Hydrolysis is the reverse of condensation: it adds water to break molecules down, while condensation joins molecules by removing water.
Metal ions in water form aqua ions that act as acids; trivalent Al3+ and Fe3+ are weak acids with pKa comparable to acetic acid, while Na+ hydrolyses almost imperceptibly.
In acid sulfate soils, loosely bound Al3+ and Fe3+ and sparingly soluble sulfates such as jarosite release H+ by hydrolysis, adding titratable and retained acidity.
In alkali soils the carbonate anion hydrolyses in water to bicarbonate and hydroxyl ions, raising pH.
Urease catalyzes hydrolysis of urea, and highly alkaline soils (pH about 8.2 or higher) increase urea hydrolysis.

The lab manual says all minerals weather by hydrolysis, which is the primary reaction releasing most plant nutrient elements from minerals; orthoclase and water yield an aluminum silicate, K+ and OH-.

sources.title: 2.1: Introduction - Geosciences LibreTexts (Introduction to Soil Science Laboratory Manual (Schwyter and Vaughan))

definition.text: Carbonic acid forms when CO2 from root and microbial respiration reacts with soil water, and is the most common acid in soils.

facts.text: It is a weak acid: at pH below 6 its ionization to H+ and bicarbonate favors the left, so few acidic hydrogen ions form.
Rainwater and CO2 keep supplying it, so it steadily accelerates mineral decomposition as water percolates.
Percolating rain carries bicarbonate downward and leaves H+ on soil surfaces, so by mass action the soil slowly acidifies over weathering time.

sources.title: 2.1: Introduction - Geosciences LibreTexts (Introduction to Soil Science Laboratory Manual (Schwyter and Vaughan))

definition.text: In a wet climate carbonation dissolves calcite and leaching removes calcium, leaving the surface soil acidic and depleted of cations.

facts.text: Calcite plus carbonic acid gives soluble calcium bicarbonate, which supplies Ca2+ to plants or is leached to groundwater and streams.
Loss of calcite from limestone leads to acidic soils, carbonate hardpans and underground caverns, and calcium bicarbonate makes limestone groundwater hard.
The same leaching depletes magnesium, potassium and sodium released by mineral hydrolysis, lowering plant nutrition and fertility.

sources.title: 2.1: Introduction - Geosciences LibreTexts (Introduction to Soil Science Laboratory Manual (Schwyter and Vaughan))

definition.text: Freshly ground glacial till has a high pH, called abrasion pH, because hydrolysis of the fine rock particles releases hydroxide.

facts.text: Initial till pH can be 9 or 10, then falls as the till absorbs carbon dioxide from the air.
Hydrolysis leaves soluble Ca2+ and OH- ions, giving pH above 8.3; carbonic acid then forms calcite quickly and later dissolves it as calcium bicarbonate.

sources.title: 2.1: Introduction - Geosciences LibreTexts (Introduction to Soil Science Laboratory Manual (Schwyter and Vaughan))

definition.text: Chemical decomposition goes fastest when more mineral surface area is exposed to reactions, so smaller particles weather faster.

facts.text: The number of exposed corners is the major factor in weathering rate, because a corner offers three surfaces and three edges for chemical attack.
Warm, wet environments speed chemical decomposition, and physical weathering usually precedes or accompanies it.
The smaller the original mineral, the faster hydrolysis proceeds.

sources.title: 2.1: Introduction - Geosciences LibreTexts (Introduction to Soil Science Laboratory Manual (Schwyter and Vaughan))

definition.text: Most minerals fall into seven classes by their fundamental anionic unit, with silicates by far the most common.

facts.text: Sulfides such as pyrite are readily oxidized in moist soils, and oxides such as hematite give red colors.
Carbonates such as calcite react with acid and weather easily in moist soils, dolomite is less reactive; gypsum and halite occur in desert soils.
Apatite is the only significant source of phosphorus.
Among silicates, olivine weathers most easily, quartz is hard and most resistant, muscovite resists weathering more than biotite, and augite is more susceptible than hornblende.

sources.title: 2.1: Introduction - Geosciences LibreTexts (Introduction to Soil Science Laboratory Manual (Schwyter and Vaughan))

definition.text: Minerals are identified by color, luster, cleavage or fracture, and hardness on the Mohs scale.

facts.text: Color is easy to see but unreliable, since impurities change it; quartz ranges from colorless to white, pink, purple and gray.
Luster is metallic or nonmetallic; nonmetallic surfaces may be glassy, waxy or earthy.
Cleavage is breaking along predictable planes, as in biotite (one direction), orthoclase (two) and calcite (three); quartz fractures instead.
Hardness is resistance to scratching, ranked on the Mohs scale from 1 (soft) to 10 (hard); gypsum scratches with a fingernail and quartz scratches glass.

sources.title: 2.1: Introduction - Geosciences LibreTexts (Introduction to Soil Science Laboratory Manual (Schwyter and Vaughan))

definition.text: Oxygen and silicon make up nearly three-fourths of the crust by mass and more than 90% by volume.

facts.text: Oxygen is 46.60% of crust mass and 91.97% by volume; silicon is 27.72% by mass.
The next six elements (Al, Fe, Ca, Na, K, Mg) bring the totals to about 98.5% by mass, leaving little room for the rest, including most plant nutrients.

sources.title: 2.1: Introduction - Geosciences LibreTexts (Introduction to Soil Science Laboratory Manual (Schwyter and Vaughan))

definition.text: Magma that cools slowly at depth forms intrusive rocks with large crystals; magma erupting to the surface cools fast to form extrusive rocks.

facts.text: Extrusive rocks can be glassy or microcrystalline, and explosive eruptions form pumice and volcanic ash.
Felsic rocks, rich in quartz and orthoclase, are light colored; mafic rocks, rich in calcic plagioclase, augite and hornblende, are dark.

sources.title: 2.1: Introduction - Geosciences LibreTexts (Introduction to Soil Science Laboratory Manual (Schwyter and Vaughan))

definition.text: Sedimentary rocks are clastic, made of cemented fragments of older rocks, or nonclastic, formed by chemical or biochemical precipitation.

facts.text: Clastic rocks are named by clast size: claystone, siltstone, mudstone, shale, sandstone and conglomerate.
Limestone and dolomite are the most common nonclastic sedimentary rocks; gypsum, chert and coal are others.
Most sedimentary rocks mix both types: sandstone has clastic grains held by a possibly nonclastic cement.

sources.title: 2.1: Introduction - Geosciences LibreTexts (Introduction to Soil Science Laboratory Manual (Schwyter and Vaughan))

definition.text: Metamorphic rocks form from extreme heat and pressure on earlier rock, and are foliated or nonfoliated.

facts.text: Foliated rocks have aligned minerals that give a layered look, while minerals in nonfoliated rocks are arranged equally in all directions and look massive.
Sedimentary rocks are most susceptible to metamorphosis, though any rock type can be the original.

sources.title: 2.1: Introduction - Geosciences LibreTexts (Introduction to Soil Science Laboratory Manual (Schwyter and Vaughan))
